claim: Black commercial corridors in Chicago developed inside zones of Black residential confinement defined by restrictive covenants, HOLC redlining, and contract selling.
contradictory_evidence: None on the geographic correlation; causation (captive market) is interpretation
evidence: NPS quote on State/35th as 'Wall Street of the black community'; D74 35th-67th State-to-Cottage-Grove graded hazardous with racist rationale (sibling-verified); Black Belt 'a mile wide at the most' (Chicago Detours)
notes: [S/N] Core causal finding; graded SUPPORTED not VERIFIED because the 'captive market' mechanism is inferred from demographic + policy evidence
source: NPS Black Metropolis Thematic Nomination (1985) via IIT Bronzeville History Booklet; CTL-DR-BCI-001 covenant/contract-selling claims; HOLC area D74 description (CTL-DR-PLACE-001); Chicago Detours on Black Belt boundaries
source_type: government record (NPS) + sibling research + specialist secondary

claim: 'The Stroll' (State Street) was the best-known Black entertainment street in America in the 1910s-20s, rivaled only by Harlem's Seventh and Lenox avenues.
evidence: Direct quote from EEChicagohistory excerpt: 'the best-known street in African American culture, rivaled only by Seventh and Lenox avenues'
notes: [N] Single-source; peer-reviewed encyclopedia entry
source: Electronic Encyclopedia of Chicago via chicago-history-resources.org

claim: The Stroll's boundaries are disputed: 26th-29th vs. 26th-39th vs. 31st-39th.
contradictory_evidence: The sources themselves are the contradiction
evidence: Four independent sources give different boundaries
notes: [N] No fixed boundary should be drawn without qualification
source: Chicago Detours (26th-29th); Electronic Encyclopedia of Chicago (26th-39th); bronzecommhub (31st-39th); IIT booklet (beginning at 31st heading south)

claim: State Street became the Stroll because it was the biggest thoroughfare through the narrow, mile-wide Black Belt and 'the natural meeting point' of its residents.
evidence: Direct quote: 'As the biggest thoroughfare in that narrow strip of land, State Street became the natural meeting point for Bronzeville's residents'
notes: [N] Container mechanism applied to the Stroll

claim: NPS (1985): 'Beginning with the establishment of the black-owned Binga Bank at 3633 South State Street in 1908, the vicinity of State and 35th streets was rapidly transformed into the Wall Street of the black community.'
evidence: Direct quotation
notes: [N] Strongest single evidence for the 35th Street corridor's identity and Black-capital exception
source: NPS Black Metropolis Thematic Nomination (1985), quoted in IIT Bronzeville History Booklet (2024)

claim: The Regal Theater (4719 S. Parkway) opened February 4, 1928, built by the National Theater Corporation, sold to Balaban & Katz in 1931, and was not Black-owned until S. B. Fuller's 1961 purchase; demolished 1973.
evidence: Sibling-verified; address confirmed by Commons category metadata (4719 S. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Drive)

claim: The Savoy Ballroom (4733 S. Parkway) opened November 1927; closing year disputed (1948 vs. 1954).
evidence: Sibling preserves both dates as alternatives

claim: The 47th Street CTA Green Line station at 314 E. 47th opened August 15, 1892.
evidence: Station infobox + article text; consistent with South Side Elevated history
notes: [N] Graded SUPPORTED (encyclopedia-only); three blocks east of State per moderncities.com

claim: Timuel Black (oral history, 2001): Bronzeville's 'downtown' was 35th and State early in the 20th century; 'by the end of the Depression, 47th Street was the heart and soul of the area.'
evidence: Direct quotation from interview with historian Timuel Black
notes: [N] Single oral-history source; underpins the 35th-to-47th 'downtown' shift
source: Daily Northwestern, 'Bronzeville: A struggle for identity' (2001-10-17)

claim: South Side Trust and Savings Bank built 1922 at 47th & Cottage Grove ($350,000), closed June 6, 1931; Chicago Landmark 2008; not Black-owned but reinforced 47th's commercial reputation.
evidence: Landmark report details (architect Albert A. Schwartz, Classical Revival, $350,000, name change from South Side State bank)
notes: [N] Documents white-financed anchor on a Black corridor
source: chicagosouthsider.com (2025); City of Chicago landmark designation report (2008)

claim: 63rd & Halsted was 'the second-busiest shopping district in Chicago' — widely repeated, but the original metric and primary source are untraced.
evidence: Sibling records as PROVISIONAL; no primary source found
notes: [S] Repeated here, not asserted; see brief §19
source: CTL-DR-PLACE-001 (LISC 2005 plan as most credible repeater)

claim: Sears at 63rd & Halsted: opening date disputed (1929/$1.5M vs. 1934/seven stories/fully air-conditioned); closed January 1976.
evidence: Sibling preserves both opening accounts; Tribune documented closure

claim: Wieboldt's stood at 63rd & Green, not 63rd & Halsted — correcting a common error.
evidence: Sibling verified against the Halsted claim

claim: Englewood went from ~69% Black in 1960 (most 'around 63rd Street') to 99% by 1980.
evidence: Sibling-verified census figures
notes: [S] The succession that made 63rd a Black corridor

claim: No verifiable evidence was found for Black-owned banks, insurers, doctors, dentists, lawyers, or real-estate offices on 63rd Street (1940s-70s) in web sources.
contradictory_evidence: None — absence of evidence, not evidence of absence
evidence: Sibling records explicit negative finding
notes: [S] Highest-value gap; needs directories/Defender archives

claim: Madison Street was known as the 'Equator of Chicago' and the 'Heart of the West Side.'
evidence: Direct quotation in investigation
notes: [N] Single strong source; nickname corroborates corridor significance

claim: Madison Street's commercial district grew 1914-1929 (Marbro Theater, 3,600 seats; Graemere Hotel) as the financial center of East and West Garfield Park, following a 1905 elevated line.
evidence: Narrative account of transit-driven white commercial development
notes: [N] Single source; supports succession model stage 1

claim: In April 1968, violence consumed a 28-block stretch of West Madison Street (additional damage on Roosevelt Road); 36 major fires were reported April 5 between 4 and 10 p.m.; 11 dead, ~500 injured by April 7.
evidence: Consistent figures across three sources
notes: [N] Graded SUPPORTED due to encyclopedia reliance for the headline figure
source: en.wikipedia.org 1968 Chicago riots; CJR (2018); Catholic New World (2008)

claim: Post-1968 rebuild programs on Madison Street failed: they 'emphasized clearing blight over building anew' and were 'too scattered, too small and too susceptible to shifting politics to make a lasting impact.'
evidence: Investigation's findings on federal/city programs; Durham's Appliances letter; Danny Davis quote
notes: [N] Core evidence for policy-driven non-recovery

claim: 79th Street 'connected many working- and middle-class neighborhoods with miles of businesses.'
evidence: Direct quotation
notes: [N] Supports far-South-Side corridor inclusion

claim: Independence Bank at 79th & Cottage Grove was Black-owned, co-founded 1964 by George Johnson (Johnson Products); sold to Shore Bank in 1995.
evidence: Direct account of bank founding, location, and sale
notes: [N] Anchor institution for the 79th corridor

claim: The Jackson Park el branch ran directly over 63rd Street (not in alleys); Dorchester station closed Jan 13, 1973; branch truncated March 4, 1982; full Green Line closed for rebuilding Jan 9, 1994-May 12, 1996; structure east of Cottage Grove demolished Sept 27, 1997.
evidence: Sibling-verified dates
notes: [S] Transit withdrawal compounding corridor decline

claim: The Dan Ryan Expressway, opened 1962, became a documented 14-lane barrier along the Black Belt's western edge.
evidence: Sibling-verified

claim: Adolph Parker opened his furniture store on S. Cottage Grove in 1934 and grew it through Depression-era credit relationships; the fourth generation still runs it at 4238 S. Cottage Grove.
evidence: Family-business oral history via LISC
notes: [N] Ordinary-merchant evidence for the Cottage Grove corridor

claim: Corridors like 59th Street and 63rd Street in Englewood were 'once thriving commercial corridors, first Italian or Polish, then Black' — commercial succession is the documented sequence.
evidence: Direct quotation on succession sequence
notes: [N] Supports Finding 2 (succession, not founding)

claim: The far-South-Side corridors (79th/87th/95th) are automobile-era strips serving a suburbanizing Black middle class; their form (shopping centers, drive-through banks) follows the residential form (bungalows, single-family homes).
contradictory_evidence: None, but causal formulation is interpretive
evidence: Convergent anchor-level evidence across sources
notes: [N] Graded PROVISIONAL per the task's causation discipline
source: Analyst synthesis of: newcity (Chatham bungalows + banks), sixthward/ninthward blogs (Target 2002, Jewel-Osco 1974), CMAP Roseland report (Michigan Ave + 95th/103rd/111th corridors)
source_type: analyst synthesis of specialist secondary + government data

claim: The transit-causation claim — that 'L' lines caused Black commercial corridors — is graded PROVISIONAL: station-corridor adjacency is verified, but every line predates Black settlement and served white riders first.
evidence: Station dates VERIFIED (1892 47th; 1905-1907 Englewood branch); Black peaks from census/sibling data
notes: [N] Central causation qualifier of this brief; see §09
source: Analyst assessment across CTA station dates (1892-1907) vs. corridor Black peaks (1920s-1960s)

claim: Roosevelt Road (12th Street) and Lake Street functioned as West Side Black commercial corridors but lack developed corridor histories in the sources consulted.
evidence: Mentions only, no corridor-level documentation found
notes: [N] Flagged for follow-up research, not asserted as corridors
source: 1968 riot damage reports (Roosevelt Road mentioned); Lake Street elevated adjacency to Madison corridor

claim: Chatham Village Square at 87th & Cottage Grove: Target opened 2002; earlier anchors included Polk Brothers, Woolworth's, a bowling alley; a fire preceded redevelopment.
evidence: Resident recollection + YoChicago video reference
notes: [N] Anchor-level evidence for the 87th corridor; blog source limits grade

claim: Corridors with Black anchor institutions retained commercial identity after retail declined; retail-only corridors left almost no institutional trace.
evidence: Contrast between landmarked 35th/47th anchors and erased 63rd/Madison retail cores
notes: [N] Finding 5; graded PROVISIONAL as interpretation
source: Analyst synthesis: 35th/47th (banks, Bee, Defender, landmarks) vs. 63rd & Halsted / Madison (no surviving institutional trace)
